record.paper_title: Open problems on billiards and geometric optics
record.original_question: For the same lattice-click model coming from translating a plane curve through an ε-sized square lattice, is there an analogue of a Fourier transform that extracts the curvature-induced patterns hidden in the cloud of click data?

evidence.quote: Question 2: The problem is that all these clicks are dumped on the segment; is there a “Fourier transform” which extracts the “curvature-induced patterns from a cloud of clicks?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Fix ε > 0 and consider the square lattice (ε ℤ)^2 ⊂ ℝ^2. Let γ ⊂ ℝ^2 be a smooth plane curve (for instance, a smooth simple closed curve, or a compact smooth arc), and for each translation vector v ∈ ℝ^2 let γ + v denote the translate of γ. Define the lattice-click set associated with γ to be the set of pairs

   C_ε(γ) := { (v, p) ∈ ℝ^2 × (ε ℤ)^2 : p ∈ γ + v },

equivalently, for each lattice point p ∈ (ε ℤ)^2 record the set of translations v for which the translated curve passes through p (a "click"). After projecting along a chosen direction (say, recording, as v moves along a fixed line, the sequence of times/positions at which any lattice point lies on γ + v), one obtains a "cloud of clicks" supported on a one-dimensional segment.

The geometric problem: the local density and fine structure of this click cloud encode geometric invariants of γ, in particular its curvature κ(s) as a function of arclength. However, the clicks coming from different parts of γ are superimposed on the same one-dimensional segment, obscuring this information.

Question. Is there an analogue of a Fourier transform — that is, an explicit integral transform, or a more general linear/nonlinear functional of the click cloud C_ε(γ) — which, applied to the cloud, extracts the curvature-induced patterns of γ? More precisely, construct a transform T such that T(C_ε(γ)) reveals (asymptotically as ε → 0, or in a suitable scaling limit) the curvature function κ of γ, separating contributions from different points of γ that otherwise pile up on the segment.
artifact.status_search_result: The question appears in a list of open problems on billiards and geometric optics, posed as an informal question about whether such a transform exists. No subsequent literature resolving it was located.
